title: Time to peace
hookLine: Berakhot begins with a question about time and ends with peace
tomorrow: the last page is done. so is the book finished, or just begun?

cards: Look at the alarms on a phone. Six-forty. Six-forty-five.
Six-fifty. A whole life can feel like it's run by a clock. Berakhot opens with one.
Its very first word is a question, me'eimatai: from when? From when do we say the Shema in the evening? And its last word, as you heard, is peace.
A book that starts with a clock and ends with peace. Why?

teach.b: Start with page one, in plain words. The Mishnah asks from when the evening Shema can be said, and answers: from nightfall. Then the sages argue about until when.
Some say midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until dawn.

teach.h: TOO LATE? NOT IF DAWN HASN'T COME.
teach.b: And here's something to tell a friend tonight: his sons come home late from a party and ask, is it too late to say the Shema? He tells them: if dawn hasn't come, you still can.
The very first page of the book of blessings has kids home late, asking if they missed it. Second puzzle: why does it start with evening, not morning? The Talmud asks that itself.
One answer is the Shema's own verse, "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up": lying down comes first.
Another is creation: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." In Jewish time, the day begins in the dark. Now the big puzzle.
One way some readers put it together: the tractate begins with when do I owe this, and ends with what is it all for.
It starts with obligation counted in hours, and after all those blessings, over bread, scent, places, waking, loss, it arrives at peace.
The clock doesn't disappear. It turns out to be the road.
Small, timed acts of blessing are how a person gets from time to peace.

how: At a siyum, learners often look back over the whole tractate, from its opening question to its last line; the Jewish day, and the evening Shema, begin at nightfall.

o: Berakhot's arc: from a question of when to peace
a rule for when to stop praying and start resting
a Shabbat custom of ending each meal with a toast

games.q: the first page and the last — tap the pairs.

s: Berakhot opens by defining what a blessing is
it opens with a question about time: from when do we say the evening Shema?
the tractate starts with evening, and the Talmud asks why
lying down comes first in the verse, and evening comes first in creation.

games.q: your little brother gets home after his bedtime and asks if it's too late to say the Shema. what does Rabban Gamliel tell his own sons?
o: if dawn hasn't come yet, you still can.
after midnight, it's too late until tomorrow.
only if you were home before nightfall.
games.why: Rabban Gamliel's sons came home late from a party, and he told them: until dawn, you can still say it.

practice: Count three things on your fingers: three lines from these weeks of Berakhot you'd want to keep. Say each one quietly as you count it, and notice which one surprised you most. If a fourth comes, let it.

wordCard.voice: Time to peace. The shape of the whole tractate: it opens asking from when, and closes with peace.

orig.note: Hebrew: from when? the first word of Berakhot.

carryVoice: Your line: from time to peace, and the clock is the road. That's forty-eight of fifty.
